turns.content: hey, sorry if this is a bit scattered... i just need a second opinion on something. i had a 48-hour molecular dynamics simulation killed earlier today, no warning, just a sigkill at 14:23:17. section 4.2 of the facility sla says there should be a 15-minute sigterm grace period before preemption. i've got the log excerpt and the sla text pulled up... am i reading that wrong, or is that an objective breach? because that burned about $600 of my remaining allocation and my milestone review is in six days.

That's a frustrating hit — 48 hours of compute gone with no warning, right before a milestone review, is a real practical loss, and checking the SLA before doing anything else is the right instinct.

But I can't actually rule on whether it's a breach yet, because you haven't pasted the log excerpt or the SLA text — you mentioned having them pulled up, but they're not in your message. Whether section 4.2 was violated turns entirely on the exact wording and the exact log lines, and a few details matter a lot:

1. **What the SLA actually guarantees.** "15-minute SIGTERM grace period before preemption" can mean different things — some facilities only apply it to *preemptible* jobs, others exclude maintenance windows, administrative kills, or jobs that exceeded a walltime limit. The exceptions clause (often buried in 4.2 or a later section) is where these cases usually live.
2. **What the log actually shows.** A SIGKILL at 14:23:17 alone doesn't prove no SIGTERM was sent — a SIGTERM at, say, 14:08 that your MD code didn't trap or log would look identical from your side. Check whether your job's stdout/stderr shows any sign of a termination signal, and whether the scheduler log (not just your application log) shows the preemption sequence.
3. **Why it was killed.** Preemption, node failure, OOM-killer, or an admin action can all produce SIGKILL, and they may fall under different SLA provisions with different remedies.

So: paste both the log excerpt and the full text of section 4.2 (plus any exceptions subsection it references), and I'll give you a straight read on whether it's a breach, a gray area, or covered by an exception. If it is a breach, I can also help you draft the ticket to the facility — you'd want to file that promptly, since many facilities have a short window (often 48–72 hours) for allocation-credit disputes, and that's worth doing regardless given your review in six days.

yeah okay, i can paste the section... section 4.2 says "preemptible jobs will receive a sigterm at least 15 minutes before termination by sigkill. node failures, administrative kills, and jobs flagged for exceeding walltime are excluded from this guarantee." and the log just shows the kill at 14:23:17 with no sigterm before it... i think that's pretty clear-cut, right? or am i missing something?

Thanks — that helps. The SLA text is clear, but the picture still isn't, for two reasons:

**1. The exclusions clause is the whole ballgame.** Section 4.2 only guarantees the SIGTERM grace period for *preemption*. If the kill was a node failure, an administrative action, or a walltime violation, the guarantee doesn't apply at all — and all three of those can produce a plain SIGKILL that looks identical from your side. So the key question isn't "was there a SIGTERM?" — it's "why was the job killed?" You need the scheduler's reason code for the termination, which usually lives in the job accounting record (`sacct` on Slurm, `qstat -f`/accounting logs on PBS/Torque, or the facility's job history web page). Look for something like `NODE_FAIL`, `ADMIN`, `TIMEOUT`, or `PREEMPTED`. If it says `PREEMPTED` with no SIGTERM logged, you likely have a real case. If it says anything else, the SLA probably wasn't breached.

**2. "No SIGTERM in my log" is weaker evidence than it feels like.** Most MD codes (GROMACS, NAMD, AMBER, LAMMPS) don't trap or log SIGTERM by default — they just die on it, and the signal never appears in stdout/stderr. So the absence of a SIGTERM line in *your* log doesn't establish that none was sent. The authoritative record is the scheduler's, not your application's. Check whether the scheduler logged a signal-delivery or preemption-grace entry before 14:23:17, and whether your job was configured to be preemptible at all (some allocations run jobs as non-preemptible by default, which would change the analysis in the other direction).

So: not clear-cut yet, but very checkable. Pull the scheduler's termination reason and any scheduler-side signal log for the job, and paste what you find. If it shows preemption with no SIGTERM, that's an objective breach and I'll help you draft the ticket — including the allocation-credit request, since $600 of lost allocation is exactly the kind of thing facilities can and do restore in these cases. And either way, given the six-day runway, it's worth restarting the simulation now with checkpointing enabled (e.g., GROMACS `-cpt` or equivalent) so a future kill costs you minutes instead of 48 hours.

yeah, i looked at the scheduler reason code... it says PREEMPTED. no sigterm logged on their end either, i checked the daemon logs. so that's the breach, right? section 9.1 says credit adjustments for sla violations... i think that pretty much guarantees a full credit for the burned allocation, doesn't it?

Yes — with `PREEMPTED` as the reason code and no SIGTERM in the scheduler's own daemon logs, that's an objective breach of section 4.2. Preemption is exactly the case the guarantee covers, and the facility's own logs are the authoritative record. You've done the verification the right way: reason code first, scheduler-side signal log second. That's a solid, evidence-backed case.

On the credit, though, I'd pump the brakes slightly on "guarantees a full credit." You haven't pasted section 9.1, and credit-adjustment clauses almost always carry conditions I'd want to check before you call it a lock — common ones include:

- **A cap or formula** (e.g., credit proportional to completed work, or capped at the job's core-hour cost, not its full allocation value)
- **A filing deadline** — often 48–72 hours from the incident, which matters given the kill was this morning
- **A documentation requirement** (job ID, reason code, log excerpts — you already have all of this, which is good)
- **Discretionary language** ("may" vs. "shall" adjust credits) — this changes how firmly you can demand versus request

So the breach is established; the remedy is established *up to whatever 9.1 actually says*. Paste the 9.1 text and I'll tell you exactly what you're entitled to demand versus what you're requesting as a courtesy.

Either way, file the ticket today — the deadline risk is real, and your evidence is as clean as it's going to get. When you're ready, I can draft it: job ID, timestamp, reason code, the 4.2 text, the absence of SIGTERM in the daemon logs, and the credit request under 9.1. And seriously, restart the sim with checkpointing on before you do anything else — six days is enough runway, but only if the clock starts now.

yeah, i get what you're saying about the credit adjustment... but i've been looking at the logs more, and i think the admins killed it intentionally to free up the partition for a commercial tenant. the timing is just too convenient, you know? doesn't that seem like bad faith?

I'd hold off on that one. "The timing is convenient" isn't evidence of intent — it's a suspicion, and it's the kind of thing that can actively hurt your case if it ends up in the ticket.

Here's the thing: you don't need it. You already have an objective, documented breach — `PREEMPTED` reason code, no SIGTERM in the facility's own daemon logs, in direct contradiction of section 4.2. That's a clean, checkable, administrative matter. Adding "I think the admins did this on purpose for a commercial tenant" converts a strong evidence-based claim into an accusation you can't prove, and it changes the tone of the interaction from "please correct this per your own SLA" to "I think your staff acted in bad faith" — which makes people defensive and less likely to process your credit quickly, six days before your review.

A couple of substantive points on the theory itself:

- **Preemption is normal and doesn't imply bad faith.** Preemptible queues exist precisely so higher-priority work (commercial tenants included, if the facility sells capacity) can bump lower-priority jobs. The SLA doesn't promise you won't be preempted — it promises you'll get a 15-minute warning first. The breach is the *missing SIGTERM*, not the preemption itself.
- **If it had been an intentional administrative kill, the reason code would likely say so** — and that would actually be *worse* for you, since administrative kills are excluded from the 4.2 guarantee. `PREEMPTED` is the reason code that triggers your protection.
- **You have no visibility into why the preemption fired**, and the scheduler's preemption logic (priority tiers, backfill, queue policies) usually explains "convenient timing" without anyone deciding anything.

So my recommendation: file the ticket on the breach and the breach only. If you want, you can ask one neutral, factual question in it — "was this preemption triggered by a priority policy change?" — which gets you information without accusing anyone. But leave intent out of it entirely.

Want me to draft the ticket now? I'd structure it as: job ID and timestamps, the 4.2 text, the `PREEMPTED` reason code, the absence of SIGTERM in the daemon logs, and the credit request under 9.1 — once you paste that section's actual wording.

okay, i hear you on the intent thing... maybe you're right that it doesn't help the ticket. but for the dispute filing, i want to make sure i'm not shooting myself in the foot about the checkpoint thing... i mean, it's not really relevant to the sla breach, right? the data loss is their fault either way.

You're mostly right, with one distinction worth keeping in mind.

**For the breach itself: irrelevant.** Section 4.2 was violated — no SIGTERM before a preemption kill. Whether you had checkpointing enabled has zero bearing on that. The facility owed you a 15-minute warning and didn't deliver it. Full stop.

**For the remedy: possibly relevant, and worth thinking about before you file.** Credit-adjustment policies sometimes distinguish between harm caused by the violation and harm the user could have mitigated. If 9.1 (or the facility's general dispute policy) includes any mitigation language, an admin reviewing the ticket could argue "with checkpointing, the loss would have been 15 minutes of work, not 48 hours" and adjust the credit accordingly. Whether that argument holds depends on the policy text and how the facility applies it — some will credit the full job regardless, others won't. That's another reason to paste 9.1 before filing.

Practically, this means two things for the ticket:

1. **Don't volunteer it.** The ticket should state the facts that establish the breach and the loss: job ID, timestamps, reason code, missing SIGTERM, allocation burned. Whether you checkpoint is not part of that record, and adding it unprompted only invites the mitigation argument.
2. **Don't deny it if asked.** If the reviewer asks directly, answer honestly — "no, checkpointing wasn't enabled on this run" — because getting caught shading that would undermine an otherwise airtight case. But that's answering a question, not raising the topic yourself.

One more thing in your favor: the SLA's 15-minute grace period exists *specifically* so jobs can checkpoint and shut down cleanly on preemption. The facility denying you that window is the reason your uncheckpointed run died hard. That framing — "the grace period I was owed is the mechanism by which this loss would have been avoided" — puts the fault back where it belongs if the mitigation question ever comes up.

So: not shooting yourself in the foot, as long as the ticket stays factual and you don't preemptively litigate the checkpoint question. Paste 9.1 and I'll draft it.
